content: 1. For smaller babies, breastfeeding is even more critical than for larger babies. 2. The appearance of breast milk changes over time: in the first few days, it is thick and yellow (colostrum), and later it becomes thinner and whiter. Both types of milk are beneficial for the baby. 3. Small babies may not feed as effectively as larger babies in the initial days. They may tire easily, suck weakly, feed for shorter periods before resting, fall asleep during feeding, take long pauses between suckling, and may not always wake up for feeds. 4. Breastfeeding becomes easier as the baby grows and suckles more effectively, stimulating the breast. 5. Skin-to-skin contact between the mother and baby facilitates breastfeeding and should be encouraged. Supporting the Mother: 6. Initiate breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. 7. Feed the baby every 2-3 hours, waking the baby for feeding if they do not wake up on their own within 2 hours of the last feed. 8. Always begin feeding with breastfeeding before offering expressed milk via a cup. 9. To improve milk flow, the mother can express a small amount of milk before attaching the baby to the breast. 10. Keep the baby at the breast for longer periods, allowing for long pauses or slow feeds. Do not interrupt the feed if the baby is still trying to suckle. 11. If the baby is not suckling well or long enough, alternative methods can be used: The mother can express breast milk directly into the baby’s mouth. The mother can express milk and feed the baby using a cup. 12. On the first day, expressed colostrum can be fed to the baby using a spoon. 13. Teach the mother to observe the baby’s swallowing when giving expressed milk. Breastfeeding Twins: 14. Reassure the mother that she can produce enough milk for two babies. 15. Encourage her to be patient, as twins may take longer to establish breastfeeding, especially if they are preterm or have low birth weight. 16. Start feeding one baby at a time until breastfeeding is well-established. 17. If one twin is weaker, ensure that the weaker twin receives enough milk. If necessary, express milk for the weaker twin and feed them by cup after initial breastfeeding. Expressing Breast Milk: 18. The mother should use clean containers (e.g., wide-necked jars, bowls, or cups) to collect and store milk. 19. Once expressed, the milk should be stored in a container with a well-fitting lid. 20. Teach the mother how to express milk herself, ensuring she: Washes her hands thoroughly. Sits or stands comfortably with a clean container beneath her breast. Places her thumb and first finger on either side of the areola, behind the nipple. Presses slightly inward toward the breast and alternates sides for at least 20-30 minutes. 21. If milk flow is poor, warm compresses, back and neck massages, or breast and nipple massages can help. 22. Expressed milk should be fed to the baby immediately or stored in a cool, clean, and safe place. 23. If necessary, repeat the process at least 8 times in 24 hours, expressing as much as the baby would take or more, every 3 hours. Feeding Expressed Milk by Cup: 24. Teach the mother to feed the baby with a cup, ensuring she: Measures the milk quantity in the cup. Holds the baby semi-upright on her lap. Rests the cup lightly on the baby’s lower lip and tips it so the milk reaches the baby’s lips without pouring it into the mouth. 25. The baby will suck the milk and swallow it. Feeding ends when the baby closes their mouth or shows no interest in taking more. 26. If the baby does not take the calculated amount, feed for a longer time or more frequently. Signs of Adequate Milk Intake: 27. The baby is satisfied after feeding. 28. Weight loss is less than 10% in the first week of life. 29. The baby gains at least 160 grams per week in subsequent weeks or a minimum of 300 grams in the first month. 30. The baby wets diapers as frequently as they are fed. Keeping the Baby Warm: 31. At birth, ensure the delivery room is warm (25-28°C) with no drafts. 32. Dry the baby immediately after birth and place them on the mother’s abdomen or a warm surface. 33. Encourage skin-to-skin contact for at least 2 hours after birth. 34. If the mother cannot provide skin-to-skin contact, wrap the baby in warm, dry clothing and place them in a cot with a blanket. 35. Assess the baby’s warmth every 4 hours by touching their feet. If cold, use skin-to-skin contact, add extra blankets, and reassess. 36. At home, explain to the mother that babies need one more layer of clothing than adults. Keep the room warm, especially in cold climates. Rewarming a Cold Baby: 37. Remove the baby’s cold clothing and place them skin-to-skin on the mother’s chest, dressed in a pre-warmed shirt, nappy, hat, and socks. 38. Cover the baby with the mother’s clothes and an additional pre-warmed blanket. 39. Check the baby’s temperature every hour until it normalizes. 40. Encourage the mother to maintain skin-to-skin contact as long as possible, especially for small babies. Additional Breastfeeding Support: 41. For mothers not breastfeeding due to illness or other reasons, teach them to express milk and feed the baby by cup. 42. If the baby does not have a mother, provide donated heat-treated breast milk or formula by cup. 43. Advise mothers who are not breastfeeding at all on how to relieve engorgement, such as using a well-fitting bra, applying warm or cold compresses, and expressing small amounts of milk to relieve discomfort. Monitoring Weight Gain: 44. Weigh the baby daily if they are small or ill, and assess weight gain regularly. 45. Use a precise and accurate scale, calibrated daily, to monitor weight changes. 46. Acceptable weight loss in the first week is up to 10%, with a daily gain of at least 15 grams thereafter. These detailed instructions ensure optimal care for newborns, particularly those who are small, preterm, or have special feeding needs.
